section_title: How should leaders be honored and held accountable?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 17 Elders who lead effectively are worthy of double honor, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching. 18 For the Scripture says, “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain,” and, “The worker is worthy of his wages.”

19 Do not entertain an accusation against an elder, except on the testimony of two or three witnesses. 20 But those who persist in sin should be rebuked in front of everyone, so that the others will stand in fear of sin. 21 I solemnly charge you before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels to maintain these principles without bias, and to do nothing out of partiality. 22 Do not be too quick in the laying on of hands and thereby share in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure.

23 Stop drinking only water and use a little wine instead, because of your stomach and your frequent ailments. 24 The sins of some men are obvious, going ahead of them to judgment; but the sins of others do not surface until later. 25 In the same way, good deeds are obvious, and even the ones that are inconspicuous cannot remain hidden.

context_lines: Paul calls for honor toward elders who lead effectively, especially those laboring in preaching and teaching. He supports that instruction with Scripture about the working ox and the worker’s wages, bringing material support into the discussion.

Honor is joined to accountability. Accusations require witness-supported grounds, and those persisting in sin are to be corrected publicly. Timothy receives a solemn charge to act without bias or favoritism.

The warning against laying on hands too quickly fits the concern for careful judgment and shared responsibility. The closing verses explain why patience matters: some sins are obvious, others appear later, and good deeds also come to light.

Paul also briefly gives personal advice about Timothy’s stomach and frequent ailments, telling him to use a little wine. The larger instruction remains careful care for the community, its servants and the truth they teach.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly understand the honor to include practical support for faithful leaders, alongside fair correction. [Wesley’s note on verse 17](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-first-epistle-to-timothy/) speaks of more generous provision. [Calvin’s comments](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/1_timothy/5.htm) likewise include support and discuss how the comparison with honor for widows bears on the phrase. Neither the office’s name nor a claim to it replaces faithful work.

The laying on of hands is commonly read as appointment to ministry. [Wesley’s note on verse 22](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-first-epistle-to-timothy/) stresses prior testing; the [USCCB notes](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/1timothy/5) also record the alternative reading of reconciliation after public sin. Both readings connect the warning with responsibility and careful judgment. The letter keeps honor, correction and impartiality together.
god_plan_lines: [1 Corinthians 9:7–14](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/9.htm) explicitly applies the working-ox instruction to support for gospel workers. Provision for ministry serves the sharing of spiritual good with the community.

[1 Corinthians 4:1–5](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_corinthians/4.htm) describes servants accountable to the Lord, who brings hidden things and motives to light. That future judgment gives weight to present faithfulness and to the refusal of favoritism. Human judgment must be careful in view of the Lord who knows fully.
